result.summary: A scorned suitor prays that Narcissus may love without possessing, and Rhamnusia grants it. Narcissus sees his reflection in a pure spring and falls in love with it, wasting away while Echo mourns him. At his death the nymphs find only a yellow and white flower.

scenes.title: The curse and the spring
scenes.summary: A spurned lover prays that Narcissus may love in vain, and Rhamnusia assents. A pristine, untouched spring is described.
scenes.stakes: Narcissus is doomed to love what he cannot have.

place.name: the clear spring in the wood

scenes.title: Narcissus loves his reflection
scenes.summary: Tired from hunting, Narcissus drinks and falls in love with his reflection. He laments to the woods, realises it is himself, and begs the image to stay.
scenes.stakes: Narcissus's obsession is consuming his life.

scenes.title: Narcissus wastes away
scenes.summary: He beats his breast, and pines like wax in fire. Echo, though angry, echoes his sorrow and his last farewell, and he dies.
scenes.stakes: Narcissus's life; Echo's grief for him.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Nemesis, goddess of retribution, from her shrine at Rhamnus.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous paradox of Narcissus: possession has made him poor.
The curse that sets Narcissus's fate in motion.
The moment he recognises the reflection as himself.

analysis.text: The story explores self-absorption and illusion: Narcissus mistakes an image for a body, and his love is both unreturnable and self-destroying.
Divine retribution for cruelty in love links this tale with Echo's, completing the pair of scorned lovers.

legacy.text: The tale gave the word narcissism and the flower name narcissus; Freud's concept of narcissism is named after it.

fun_facts.text: In Ovid's telling the seer Tiresias had predicted Narcissus would live long only if he never knew himself.

language_notes.text: The unnamed spurned person is the male or female rejected lover; the curse mirrors Narcissus' own coldness: may he love and not possess.
Rhamnusia is Nemesis, goddess of retribution, named from her shrine at Rhamnus in Attica. She punishes arrogance, so she grants the prayer.
Parian marble came from the island of Paros and was prized by sculptors for its pure white color.
Bacchus (god of wine) and Apollo were both imagined as ideally beautiful, with lovely hair; the comparison praises Narcissus' fingers and locks.
"Plenty has made me poor" is a paradox: possessing the beloved's image, he cannot actually have him.
Hoar frost: white frost that covers the ground in the morning and melts in the sun.
Stygian waters: the river Styx, one of the rivers of the underworld, where the dead were received.
Cutting off hair and laying it on the dead was an ancient Greek and Roman mourning custom.
The shaken torches were brandished to kindle the pyre; torches and a bier were standard parts of an ancient funeral.

context_notes.text: This heading is a summary added by the translator; the flower is the narcissus.
Narcissus had already rejected the nymph Echo and others; this sentence summarizes his pattern of cruelty to admirers.
The untouched spring sets apart a secluded, almost sacred place, typical of Ovid's settings where transformations occur.
Echo, a nymph, was earlier spurned by Narcissus and wasted away until only her voice remained, which can only repeat others' last words.
The Naiads are freshwater nymphs, here called his sisters because his mother Liriope was a water nymph; Dryads are tree nymphs.

literary_notes.text: Silver-bright, untouched water suggests purity and stillness, preparing for a mirror-like surface.
A second 'thirst' for his own image grows beside physical thirst, showing desire replacing a natural need.
Comparing Narcissus to a marble statue shows his stillness and foreshadows his lifeless, transformed state.
Balanced opposites, pursuing and pursued, inflaming and burning, show the lover and beloved are one person.
The narrator suddenly addresses Narcissus directly, adding pity and drawing the reader into his delusion.
Obstacles that usually part lovers are absent; only a thin layer of water divides him from his wish, which makes his torment sharper.
Narcissus finally recognizes himself, fulfilling the prophecy that he would live only if he never knew himself, so his doom is now sealed.
The reddening of his white skin is likened to apples and grapes, giving a delicate, visual image of his bruised beauty.
Narcissus is compared to wax and frost melting in warmth, showing his slow, helpless wasting away through love.
Echo's repeated word gives the only reply Narcissus ever receives, a bitter reversal of his earlier rejection of her.
The flower, white petals around a yellow center, becomes the lasting emblem of his beauty and self-love.
